C90B Fuel System Overview
A complete understanding of the fuel system is essential for safe and confident aircraft operation.
Fuel management is a major daily responsibility for the pilot.
The aircraft has two independent fuel systems,
one for each engine,
connected by a crossfeed system.
Total usable fuel is three hundred eighty four gallons.
There are three modes of operation.
Normal operation.
Each engine receives fuel from its own tanks,
using its own boost pump.
Automatic crossfeed.
If a boost pump fails,
fuel pressure drops,
and the system automatically opens the crossfeed valve.
The remaining boost pump supplies both engines.
Suction feed.
If needed,
the engine driven pump can draw fuel without boost pressure.
This is limited to ten hours total use.
Each wing contains multiple tanks.
Fuel flows from wing tanks,
to the center tank,
then to the nacelle tank.
Engines are fed directly from the nacelle tank.
Fuel transfer is mostly automatic.
When the nacelle tank drops about ten gallons,
transfer pumps refill it from the wing tanks.
If transfer pressure is not detected,
a no fuel transfer warning appears.
This may mean either empty wing tanks,
or a pump failure.
If transfer pumps fail,
gravity feed will still move most fuel to the nacelle tank.
Boost pumps provide fuel pressure to the engine.
Low pressure triggers a fuel pressure warning.
Operation without boost pumps is limited to ten hours.
Both boost pumps must be working before takeoff.
The crossfeed system allows one side to feed both engines.
It is used only during engine failure,
or boost pump failure.
In automatic mode,
the system responds to pressure loss without pilot input.
The firewall shutoff valves control fuel flow to each engine.
Open allows fuel flow.
Closed stops all fuel to the engine.
Fuel quantity is measured using a capacitance system.
It reads fuel in pounds,
and compensates for temperature and density changes.
Pilots can select total fuel,
or nacelle tank fuel only.
Fuel venting prevents tank collapse.
Heated vents and ram air vents provide redundancy.
Fuel drains must be checked before flight.
Water and contaminants collect in low points.
Jet fuel requires longer settling time,
up to three hours.
Fuel contamination is a major concern.
Water can freeze at low temperatures,
forming ice in the system.
Fuel heating reduces icing risk,
but anti icing additives may still be required.
Good fuel handling practices are critical.
Use clean fuel sources,
allow time for settling,
and always check for contamination.
Microbial growth can occur in contaminated fuel.
Biocide additives may be used to prevent this.
Approved fuels include jet fuels,
and aviation gasoline for emergency use only.
Use of aviation gasoline is limited,
due to engine wear and performance effects.
When fueling,
fill nacelle tanks first,
then wing tanks.
This ensures proper fuel distribution.
Always ground the aircraft during fueling,
and check for contamination after fueling.
Fuel system operation is mostly automatic.
The pilot’s role is monitoring,
verification,
and proper response to warnings.
Key risks include:
boost pump failure,
fuel contamination,
and improper fuel management.
Proper understanding and monitoring of the system ensures safe and efficient flight operations.
